metals-001.question: What does the JIS steel designation “S45C” stand for?
choices: A rolled steel for general structure with a tensile strength of at least 450 MPa
A carbon steel for machine structural use with about 0.45% carbon
A cast iron with about 4.5% carbon
metals-001.explanation: In S45C, S stands for steel and C for carbon, and the number in between gives the nominal carbon content in units of 0.01%, so it is a carbon steel for machine structural use containing about 0.45% carbon (roughly 0.42–0.48%), close to AISI 1045. Its strength can be adjusted by quenching and tempering, and it is widely used for shafts and gears. In SS400 (JIS), the rolled steel for general structure, the number gives not the carbon content but the guaranteed tensile strength (at least 400 MPa), so the choice reading S45C as rolled steel for general structure with a tensile strength of at least 450 MPa confuses how the two designations are read. Above 2.14% carbon the material is no longer steel but cast iron, and 4.5% is the mistake of reading the number in units of 0.1%. In the hypoeutectoid range, more carbon means higher hardness and strength but lower ductility and weldability.

metals-002.question: Which correctly describes the properties of the 18%Cr-8%Ni austenitic stainless steel SUS304 (JIS; equivalent to AISI 304)?
choices: Its high Cr content makes it a martensitic stainless steel, so it hardens greatly on quenching in oil or water
Despite its Ni content it is a BCC ferritic steel, strongly attracted to a magnet even in the annealed condition
It is FCC austenite, does not harden on quenching, and is nearly nonmagnetic in the annealed condition
metals-002.explanation: SUS304 contains about 8% Ni, which stabilizes austenite, so it keeps an FCC austenitic structure even at room temperature. Because it does not transform on cooling, it does not harden by quenching; it is strengthened by cold working instead. In the annealed condition it is nearly nonmagnetic, but heavy cold working converts part of it to strain-induced martensite, and it becomes attracted to a magnet. Being FCC, it shows no ductile-to-brittle transition at low temperatures and can be used for cryogenic vessels. Steels that harden on quenching are martensitic grades such as SUS420J2 (similar to AISI 420), with about 13% Cr and higher carbon. Ferritic grades such as SUS430 (AISI 430) contain almost no Ni and are BCC and strongly magnetic.

metals-003.question: Which correctly pairs a copper alloy with its main alloying element?
choices: Brass and Zn (zinc)
Bronze and Ni (nickel)
Cupronickel and Sn (tin)
metals-003.explanation: Brass is copper with zinc added. 70/30 brass (cartridge brass), with about 30% Zn, consists only of the FCC α phase and is very ductile, which suits deep drawing. 60/40 brass (Muntz metal), with about 40% Zn, contains the BCC β phase; it is stronger but less cold-workable. Bronze is copper with tin added; it has good castability and wear resistance and is used for bearings and castings. Cupronickel is copper with nickel added; it resists seawater and is used for heat-exchanger tubes and coins. The choices pairing bronze with Ni and cupronickel with Sn swap the alloying elements of bronze and cupronickel. Because brass contains zinc, in some environments dezincification, the selective leaching of zinc alone, must be watched for.

metals-004.question: In the aluminum alloy designation “A6061-T6” (JIS; 6061-T6 in Aluminum Association notation), what treatment does “T6” indicate?
choices: Solution heat-treated and then naturally aged at room temperature
Solution heat-treated and then artificially aged
Work-hardened by cold working
metals-004.explanation: In aluminum alloy designations, the four-digit number gives the alloy series (the 6000 series is Al-Mg-Si) and the temper designation after the hyphen gives the processing condition. T6 means solution heat-treated and quenched, then artificially aged by heating to about 150–200 °C, strengthened by fine Mg₂Si-type precipitates. Solution heat-treated and naturally aged at room temperature is T4, somewhat weaker than T6. Work hardening by cold working is designated H and is used for non-heat-treatable alloys such as the 5000 series. In addition, O means annealed (the softest condition) and F means as-fabricated. Because strength varies widely with temper even for the same alloy, drawings specify both.

metals-005.question: Which statement about the crystal structure of pure titanium is correct?
choices: It is the HCP α phase at room temperature and changes to the BCC β phase above about 882 °C
It is BCC at room temperature and changes to the FCC γ phase above about 912 °C
It remains a single FCC phase at all temperatures, with no allotropic transformation
metals-005.explanation: Titanium takes the HCP α phase at room temperature and undergoes an allotropic transformation to the BCC β phase above about 882 °C. Al and O stabilize the α phase, while V and Mo stabilize the β phase, so depending on the alloying elements titanium alloys are classified as α, α+β or β alloys. The well-known Ti-6Al-4V is an α+β alloy whose strength can be adjusted by heat treatment, and it is used for aircraft parts. The choice of BCC at room temperature changing to FCC above about 912 °C confuses titanium with iron, which behaves that way. Being FCC at all temperatures without transforming describes aluminum and copper. Titanium has a density of about 4.5 g/cm³, about 60% that of steel, giving it a high specific strength, and its dense surface oxide film gives it excellent corrosion resistance. The HCP α phase has few slip systems, so cold working at room temperature is not as easy as in FCC metals.

metals-006.question: Which pair of solute elements forms interstitial solid solutions in iron?
choices: Ni and Cr
Mn and Si
C and N
metals-006.explanation: Carbon (C) and nitrogen (N) have atomic radii much smaller than iron, so instead of replacing iron atoms on lattice sites they enter the gaps (interstitial sites) and form interstitial solid solutions. In BCC ferrite these sites distort the lattice asymmetrically, so even small amounts strengthen strongly; they also gather around dislocations and pin them, causing the distinct yield point and strain aging of mild steel. Ni, Cr, Mn and Si are close to iron in atomic size and dissolve substitutionally, replacing iron atoms on lattice sites. A rough guide for extensive substitutional solubility is that the atomic radii differ by no more than about 15%, among other conditions (the Hume-Rothery rules).

metals-007.question: Which correctly describes recovery, which occurs when a cold-worked metal is heated to a temperature too low for recrystallization?
choices: Dislocations rearrange and internal stresses fall, but hardness and strength drop only slightly
New strain-free grains form and replace the worked ones, the dislocation density falls, and hardness drops greatly
Grain boundaries migrate and the grains coarsen to several times their size, so hardness and strength drop greatly
metals-007.explanation: Recovery is the process in which dislocations introduced by working annihilate or rearrange into lower-energy configurations (polygonization, which forms low-angle grain boundaries). Since the total number of dislocations does not drop much, hardness and strength fall only slightly, but internal (residual) stresses are reduced, and electrical resistivity recovers well as point defects are eliminated. Stress-relief annealing, used to remove only the stresses while keeping the shape of a worked part, exploits recovery. The formation of new strain-free grains, with a large drop in dislocation density and hardness, is recrystallization, which occurs at higher temperatures. Grain enlargement is grain growth, which follows recrystallization; both are stages distinct from recovery.

metals-008.question: Which sequence of solidification structures is generally seen in the cross section of an ingot made by pouring molten metal into a mold?
choices: From the outside: columnar grains, chill grains, equiaxed grains
From the outside: equiaxed grains, columnar grains, chill grains
From the outside: chill grains, columnar grains, equiaxed grains
metals-008.explanation: When the melt touches the cold mold wall, the large undercooling nucleates many crystals at once, forming a layer of fine equiaxed chill grains at the surface. Next, grains whose orientation favors growth extend selectively in the direction opposite to heat flow toward the mold wall (inward, as heat flows outward), forming a zone of elongated columnar grains pointing toward the center. In the center the temperature gradient becomes small, and equiaxed grains with no preferred direction grow from crystal fragments drifting in the liquid. The choices that start from columnar or equiaxed grains on the outside rearrange this order. Columnar grains have direction-dependent properties, and impurities tend to collect where columnar grains meet, so castings are sometimes inoculated or stirred to increase the equiaxed zone.

metals-009.question: A titanium alloy has a tensile strength of 950 MPa and a density of 4.43 g/cm³, and a high-strength steel has a tensile strength of 1200 MPa and a density of 7.85 g/cm³. About how many times the specific strength (tensile strength/density) of the steel is that of the titanium alloy?
choices: About 0.79 times
About 1.4 times
About 1.8 times
metals-009.explanation: The specific strength is 950/4.43 ≈ 214 kN·m/kg for the titanium alloy and 1200/7.85 ≈ 153 kN·m/kg for the steel, so the ratio is 214/153 ≈ 1.40, about 1.4 times (MPa divided by g/cm³ becomes kN·m/kg once units are made consistent). About 0.79 times compares only the tensile strengths (950/1200), ignoring weight. About 1.8 times takes only the density ratio (7.85/4.43 ≈ 1.77), ignoring the difference in strength. For a member carrying the same load, a higher specific strength allows a lighter design, which is why aircraft structures use titanium alloys, aluminum alloys and carbon-fiber composites. Material cost and ease of fabrication must also be weighed in the choice, however.

metals-010.question: For annealed copper, the relation between true stress σ and true strain ε in the plastic region is σ = Kεⁿ with K = 530 MPa and n = 0.44. Which value is closest to the true stress at a true strain of 0.10?
choices: About 53 MPa
About 1460 MPa
About 192 MPa
metals-010.explanation: σ = 530 × 0.10^0.44. Since 0.10^0.44 = 10^(−0.44) ≈ 0.363, σ ≈ 530 × 0.363 ≈ 192 MPa. About 53 MPa forgets the exponent and uses K × ε = 530 × 0.10. About 1460 MPa substitutes the strain as the percentage 10 (530 × 10^0.44); that it exceeds the strength coefficient K is itself a sign that something is wrong. n is called the strain-hardening exponent; the larger it is, the more readily the material strengthens as it deforms and the larger the uniform elongation before necking. Under constant volume, necking can be estimated to begin when the true strain equals n (0.44 in this example). FCC copper and austenitic stainless steels are typical examples with large n.

metals-011.question: Taking the recrystallization temperature as roughly 0.4 times the melting point (in absolute temperature), which of these counts as hot working? Take the melting points as 327 °C for lead, 3422 °C for tungsten and 1538 °C for iron.
choices: Rolling lead at room temperature (25 °C)
Rolling tungsten at 1000 °C
Rolling iron sheet at room temperature (25 °C)
metals-011.explanation: Hot and cold working are distinguished not by whether the temperature is high or low but by whether working takes place above the recrystallization temperature. For lead the guide is 0.4 × (327 + 273) = 240 K, about −33 °C, so rolling at room temperature (25 °C) counts as hot working; recovery and recrystallization proceed during working and almost no work hardening remains. For tungsten the guide is 0.4 × 3695 ≈ 1478 K (about 1205 °C), so at 1000 °C, even though it glows red, it is cold working by this criterion (working at elevated temperatures below the recrystallization temperature is sometimes called warm working). Computing 0.4 × 3422 ≈ 1369 °C in °C is wrong. For iron the guide is 0.4 × 1811 ≈ 724 K (about 451 °C), so rolling at room temperature is cold working. Actual recrystallization temperatures vary with the amount of cold work and the purity.

metals-012.question: Chvorinov's rule gives the solidification time t of a casting in terms of the ratio of its volume V to surface area A as t = B(V/A)² (B is a constant set by the mold and metal). Under the same mold conditions, a cube casting 50 mm on a side solidified in 4.0 minutes. Which value is closest to the solidification time of a cube casting 100 mm on a side?
choices: 8.0 minutes
16 minutes
32 minutes
metals-012.explanation: For a cube of side a, V/A = a³/(6a²) = a/6, so V/A ≈ 8.3 mm for 50 mm and about 16.7 mm for 100 mm, exactly twice as large. The solidification time is proportional to the square of V/A, so t = 4.0 × 2² = 16 minutes. 8.0 minutes assumes the solidification time is proportional to size, and 32 minutes assumes it is proportional to volume and multiplies by 8. Larger castings take longer to solidify and have coarser structures. Because a riser (the feeder that supplies molten metal) cannot compensate for shrinkage cavities unless it solidifies after the casting, this rule is also the basis for designing risers with a larger V/A than the casting.

metals-013.question: Which correctly describes the difference between gray cast iron and spheroidal graphite (ductile) cast iron?
choices: Gray cast iron has spheroidal graphite, so its notch effect is small and it is more ductile and tough than ductile iron
In both, all the carbon is present as cementite and there is no graphite, so the fracture surface looks white
Ductile iron, in which additions such as Mg to the melt make the graphite spheroidal, is more ductile and tough than gray iron with flake graphite
metals-013.explanation: In gray cast iron, graphite crystallizes as thin flakes. The sharp tips of the flakes act like notches that concentrate stress, so the iron is brittle in tension with almost no elongation. On the other hand, it damps vibration well and is easy to cast and machine, so it is used for machine-tool beds. In spheroidal graphite cast iron, small additions of Mg or Ce to the melt make the graphite spheroidal; the stress concentration is small, so ductility and toughness are large, and with strength approaching steel it is used for automobile parts and water pipes. The statement with the graphite shapes swapped is wrong. Carbon present as cementite with a white fracture surface describes white cast iron; the fracture surface of gray cast iron looks gray because of the graphite.

metals-014.question: What is the main reason magnesium alloys are poorly suited to cold forming such as pressing at room temperature?
choices: They are BCC, the Peierls stress grows at low temperature, and room temperature lies below their ductile-brittle transition temperature
They are HCP, and at room temperature the active slip systems are mainly limited to basal slip, giving too few independent slip systems
They are FCC, but their density is low at 1.74 g/cm³ and their atomic bonds are weak, so they crack as soon as they are worked
metals-014.explanation: Magnesium has the HCP structure, and at room temperature basal slip, which has a low resistance, is the main active mode. For a polycrystalline metal to deform to an arbitrary shape without cracking, five independent slip systems are needed, but basal slip alone provides only two, and the other systems hardly operate at room temperature, so neighboring grains cannot deform compatibly and cracks form easily. Magnesium is therefore often press-formed warm, at roughly 200°C or above, where prismatic and pyramidal slip become active, and cast parts are commonly made by die casting. Low-temperature brittleness of BCC metals is a feature of steels and does not apply to magnesium. Its density of 1.74 g/cm³, the lowest among structural metals, is real, but magnesium is not FCC.

metals-015.question: In the International Annealed Copper Standard (IACS), a resistivity of 1.7241 µΩ·cm at 20°C corresponds to 100% IACS. Which is closest to the conductivity, in % IACS, of a brass whose resistivity at 20°C is 6.2 µΩ·cm?
choices: About 28% IACS
About 72% IACS
About 360% IACS
metals-015.explanation: Conductivity is the reciprocal of resistivity, so % IACS = (1.7241/6.2) × 100 ≈ 27.8, about 28% IACS. This is close to the actual value for brass containing about 30% Zn, which conducts only about a quarter as well as pure copper. About 360% IACS inverts the resistivity ratio to 6.2/1.7241, which would make brass a better conductor than pure copper. About 72% IACS mistakes (6.2 − 1.7241)/6.2, that is, 1 minus the conductivity ratio, for the conductivity. Dissolved atoms scatter electrons and raise the resistivity greatly, so for wires and connectors, copper alloys with little solute or precipitation-strengthened copper alloys are chosen to balance strength and conductivity.

metals-016.question: Mn is added to steel to prevent the harmful effect of the sulfur (S) it contains. Which is the correct reason?
choices: Mn combines with P to form phosphides and prevents embrittlement at low temperature (cold shortness)
Mn combines with hydrogen to form hydrides and prevents fine internal cracks in the steel (flakes)
Mn combines with S to form MnS and prevents cracking during hot working caused by FeS (hot shortness)
metals-016.explanation: Sulfur forms FeS with iron, and the FeS-Fe eutectic melts at a low temperature of about 988°C, so FeS films remaining at grain boundaries melt at the higher temperatures of hot rolling or forging and the steel cracks along the boundaries. This is hot shortness (red shortness). Mn combines with S more readily than Fe does and forms MnS, which has a high melting point and is dispersed within the grains, so the cracking is prevented. This is why carbon steels generally contain added Mn; free-machining steels even use MnS deliberately to break up the chips. The main harm of P is cold shortness, which Mn does not fix, and Mn cannot bind the hydrogen that causes flakes either.

metals-017.question: Which is a characteristic of killed steel, which is solidified after thorough deoxidation with Si or Al?
choices: No CO gas bubbles form during solidification, so the steel has no internal blowholes and a uniform composition
The molten steel boils with CO bubbles during solidification, so many blowholes remain inside
The Al₂O₃ formed by deoxidation coats the grain boundaries, so the grains coarsen easily and the toughness is low
metals-017.explanation: Molten steel contains dissolved oxygen, which reacts with carbon during solidification and releases CO bubbles. In killed steel, thorough deoxidation with Si or Al removes the oxygen as SiO₂ or Al₂O₃, so the steel solidifies quietly without gas evolution and is uniform, with few blowholes and little segregation. In exchange, a shrinkage pipe forms at the top of the ingot. Steel deoxidized only weakly so that CO bubbles form during solidification is rimmed steel. In Al-deoxidized steel, fine AlN particles hinder the migration of grain boundaries, so the steel tends to be fine-grained and tough rather than coarse-grained.

metals-018.question: Which combination correctly classifies alloying elements in steel into austenite stabilizers and ferrite stabilizers?
choices: Cr, Mo and Si stabilize austenite, and Ni, Mn, C and N stabilize ferrite
Ni and Cr both stabilize austenite, and C and N stabilize ferrite
Ni, Mn, C and N stabilize austenite, and Cr, Mo and Si stabilize ferrite
metals-018.explanation: Ni, Mn, C and N widen the γ field and keep austenite stable to lower temperatures. Cr, Mo and Si (and also Ti, Nb, Al and others) widen the α field and stabilize ferrite; large additions close the γ field into a loop. The 18Cr-8Ni steel SUS304 is austenitic because Ni outweighs the ferrite-stabilizing effect of Cr, while SUS430, with about 17% Cr and no Ni, is ferritic. The structures of stainless steels are organized by Cr and Ni equivalents (the Schaeffler diagram), and Cr and Ni are the classic elements acting in opposite directions.

metals-019.question: Which is a characteristic of duplex stainless steel, consisting of roughly equal parts ferrite and austenite?
choices: It has a higher proof stress than austenitic grades and also resists chloride stress corrosion cracking
It is single-phase austenite, so it is non-magnetic and does not become brittle down to cryogenic temperatures
It contains martensite, so it is hardened by quenching and used for knives and tools
metals-019.explanation: Duplex stainless steel raises Cr to about 20-28%, reduces Ni and adds N and Mo so that ferrite and austenite are present in roughly equal amounts. The fine two-phase structure and solid-solution strengthening by nitrogen give about twice the proof stress of austenitic grades such as SUS304. It resists chloride stress corrosion cracking, the weak point of austenitic grades, and its high Cr, Mo and N contents also give good pitting resistance, so it is used in chemical plants and seawater piping. Because it contains ferrite it is magnetic and shows the ductile-to-brittle transition of ferrite at low temperature. It is not a martensitic grade and is not used hardened by quenching.

metals-020.question: For cast irons, the carbon equivalent CE = C + (Si + P)/3 (mass%), which converts the effect of Si and other elements into carbon, is compared with the Fe-C eutectic composition of 4.3% to judge whether the iron is hypoeutectic or hypereutectic. For a ductile iron with 3.8% C, 2.4% Si and 0% P, which combination of CE and judgment is correct?
choices: CE ≈ 3.8%, hypoeutectic
CE ≈ 4.6%, hypereutectic
CE ≈ 6.2%, hypereutectic
metals-020.explanation: CE = 3.8 + (2.4 + 0)/3 = 3.8 + 0.8 = 4.6%, which exceeds the eutectic composition of 4.3%, so the iron is hypereutectic. Si shifts the eutectic composition to lower carbon, so an iron that looks hypoeutectic from its carbon content alone can solidify as eutectic or hypereutectic once its Si is taken into account. CE ≈ 3.8% ignores the effect of Si, and CE ≈ 6.2% adds Si without dividing by 3. In a hypereutectic iron graphite crystallizes as the primary phase, whereas in a hypoeutectic iron primary austenite dendrites form first. CE is used in foundry control as a guide to fluidity, shrinkage and the amount of graphite.
